newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: FOCUS - Thumbs up for new Philips chief.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Thumbs up for new Philips chief.

text.p: Analysts and investors gave a provisional thumbs up on Thursday to the tough-talking new boss of Philips, Cor Boonstra, despite the company's steep drop in third quarter earnings.

They chose to focus more on his plans to overhaul the group than on results showing Philips Electronics NV's net profit from normal operations fell to 123 million guilders ($72 million) from 539 million a year ago.

But Boonstra, making a surprise appearance at a news conference, pledged that Europe's biggest consumer electronics would tackle its problems head-on, taking a one billion guilder charge in the fourth quarter for a company-wide reorganisation.
Boonstra told reporters that Philips was looking for double digit growth in income from operations next year and targeted a big rise in return on net operating capital.

"I will also take head-on what I call the bleeders in the company, that means we will turn around, sell or close businesses that are not performing to our standards or are not fitting into our portfolio," he said.

Analysts lapped up the tough talk from Boonstra, who took over as chairman from Jan Timmer on October 1, and Philips shares rallied to close 1.70 guilders higher at 58.30 after initially falling on the bigger than expected profit drop.
ING Barings analyst Eric de Graaf said Boonstra was clearly identifying problems and devising a strategy to deal with them.
"Boonstra has stated unambiguously that if activities are not performing well they will be sold or closed down... I am very positive about that," he said.

But analysts said that after setting aside almost six billion guilders on various reorganisation drives since 1990 it was time for Philips to make strategic changes in its business portfolio, rather than adopting a piecemeal approach to its problems which stem from flagging markets and price erosion.

Ad van der Laar of Bank Labouchere said Boonstra would ultimately be judged by the results he achieved, not the performance targets he set: "They (the targets) are very ambitious, to say the least. But what else can Boonstra say?"

Boonstra took pains to point out that Philips was not in the same position as it was in the early 1990s when his predecessor Timmer brought in the Centurion recovery progamme, hauling the firm back from the brink of disaster after big losses.
"The company six years ago was in a state of danger of bankruptcy. That is not the case today. We are in a financically much better position," he said.
Boonstra, a former president of U.S. consumer products giant Sara Lee Corp, joined Philips in 1994 and is the first outsider to head the company in its 105-year history.

Philips may no longer be in intensive care, bit it is still seen as limping along in international markets -- a little unfocused, not quite as competitive as the Japanese, some parts doing well and others just not living up to their potential.
Some analysts believe Boonstra, could be the man to sort that out, bringing a new shot of the killer instinct needed to make the world sit up and take notice of Philips' brands.

"He's not a Philips man. Maybe it brings a fresh approach. He's come from a background at Sara Lee that's strong on brand names, pretty good on restructuring -- all things that are relevant for Philips," one London-based analyst said as he took over at the helm earlier this month.
His stewardship at Sara Lee caused eyebrows to rise and sparks to fly as he hacked back jobs and costs, prompting mutterings about his aggressive, no-holds-barred style.
"We all know he's a man in a hurry," said one Philips insider. "He's 58 now and he's due to retire at 62 so he hasn't got that long to get some results." ($1=1.708 Guilder)
